scope: Cities and sites that act as continuous protagonists across the corpus — capitals across regimes, sacred-political centres, ashrams, founding sites.

places.name: Delhi
places.tooltip: Delhi — capital across eight regimes, 1206–present
places.summary: From Qutb-ud-din Aibak's coronation to the Republic's seat — eight regimes, two destructions, the longest continuous capital in the subcontinent.
places.framing: Delhi is the only city in the subcontinent that has been imperial capital across the Sultanate (1206–1526), the Mughal Empire (1526–1857 with the brief Agra interludes), the Raj (from 1911 when the capital shifted from Calcutta), and the Republic. Each regime built outward — Mehrauli, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Firuzabad, Shahjahanabad, New Delhi — leaving an archaeology of seven distinct city-foundations across thirteen square miles. The 1398 sack by Timur and the 1857 destruction by the British each broke the city's institutional continuity but not its political claim. The corpus reaches Delhi from twelve different campaign threads — Sultanate, Mughal, 1857, Independence, post-Republic — making it the corpus's densest gather-by-place.

sources.label: Percival Spear, Delhi: Its Monuments and History (1937; rev. 1994)
Sunil Kumar, The Present in Delhi's Pasts (2002)

places.name: Agra
places.tooltip: Agra — Mughal capital 1526–1648, then again under Aurangzeb
places.summary: Sikandar Lodi's 1504 capital became the high-Mughal seat — the city of the Akbarnama, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, the Taj, and Babur's tomb-then-relocation.
places.framing: Agra is the Mughal capital twice: under Babur, Humayun, and Akbar (1526–1571 and again from 1605), and under Aurangzeb after Shahjahanabad lost favour. Sikandar Lodi founded the modern city in 1504; the Mughal court chronicles — Baburnama, Akbarnama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri — were largely composed or finalised here. The Taj Mahal (1632–1653) is its most legible monument; the Agra Fort, the Itimad-ud-Daulah tomb, and Sikandra (Akbar's mausoleum) form the rest of the architectural record. Babur was buried at Agra in 1530 before his remains were moved to Kabul — the city is the literal foundation site of Mughal imperial geography.

sources.label: Ebba Koch, The Complete Taj Mahal (2006)

places.name: Lahore
places.tooltip: Lahore — Mughal-Sikh-Punjab capital across five centuries
places.summary: Aibak's coronation site 1206, Mughal cultural capital under Jahangir, Sikh Empire seat under Ranjit Singh — every Punjab-based regime's centre.
places.framing: Lahore is the political capital of every regime that has organised power around the western Punjab. Qutb-ud-din Aibak crowned himself sultan here in 1206 — the formal beginning of the Delhi Sultanate is technically a Lahore event. Jahangir made Lahore the Mughal cultural capital during his reign; he is buried at Shahdara across the Ravi. Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire (1801–1849) ran from the Lahore Fort. Babur took Lahore in 1524 — the last staging point before Panipat and the Mughal founding. The 1947 partition split the city's communities decisively; the Wagah border that today divides India and Pakistan is fifteen kilometres away.

sources.label: Ian Talbot, Lahore in the Time of the Raj (2013)

places.name: Calcutta
places.tooltip: Calcutta — EIC headquarters 1772–1911, then anti-colonial capital
places.summary: Job Charnock's 1690 trading post became EIC capital after Plassey, then anti-colonial centre after 1905 — the city that shaped Raj and resistance to it.
places.framing: Calcutta was the British India capital from 1772 (when Warren Hastings centralised EIC government there) until 1911 (when George V shifted the capital to Delhi). Curzon's 1905 partition of Bengal — engineered partly to break Calcutta's political weight — turned the city into the engine of the Swadeshi movement and, in succession, the Anushilan Samiti revolutionaries, the Brahmo Samaj reformers, the Tagore-Bose-Vivekananda Bengal Renaissance circuit, the early Communist Party of India, and the Direct Action Day killings of 1946. The corpus's reform-era and independence-era events anchor here as densely as Delhi's Sultanate-era ones do at Delhi.

sources.label: Sumanta Banerjee, The Parlour and the Streets: Elite and Popular Culture in Nineteenth-Century Calcutta (1989)

places.name: Bombay
places.tooltip: Bombay — EIC trading post, INC founding city, Quit India launch
places.summary: From the 1661 Portuguese-dowry trading post to the INC's 1885 founding to Gandhi's 1942 Quit India launch — Bombay is Indian political history in three acts.
places.framing: Bombay was acquired by the EIC in 1661 as Catherine of Braganza's dowry to Charles II. The seven islands were reclaimed as a single city through the eighteenth century; the railway and the cotton boom made it British India's commercial capital by 1850. The Indian National Congress was founded at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College on 28 December 1885; Gandhi delivered the Quit India speech at Gowalia Tank Maidan on 8 August 1942; Ambedkar self-published Annihilation of Caste here in 1936; the RIN Mutiny broke out in February 1946. The Bombay Plan (1944), Hindu Code Bill protests, and the Bombay film industry that became Bollywood all anchor here. After 1995 the city is officially Mumbai.

sources.label: Gyan Prakash, Mumbai Fables (2010)

places.name: Pune
places.tooltip: Pune — Maratha-Peshwa capital, then Phule and Tilak's reform-era seat
places.summary: Peshwa capital from 1714 until 1818, then the centre of Phule's anti-caste polemic, Tilak's nationalist press, and Pandita Ramabai's Sharada Sadan.
places.framing: Pune was the Peshwa capital — the de facto seat of the Maratha Confederacy from 1714 until the Anglo-Maratha War of 1818 ended Peshwa rule. The British then made it the Bombay Presidency's monsoon capital and a major army cantonment. From the 1870s Pune became the centre of three distinct reform-era currents: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj and India's first girls' school (1848), Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Kesari and Maratha newspapers radicalising the Congress, and Pandita Ramabai's Sharada Sadan and Mukti Mission for high-caste widows. Gandhi was imprisoned at the Yerwada Jail (in Pune district) for most of his post-1922 detentions; the 1932 Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar over separate electorates was negotiated there.

sources.label: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (1993)

places.name: Hyderabad
places.tooltip: Hyderabad — Qutb Shahi, Asaf Jahi (Nizam), then 1948 annexation
places.summary: Qutb Shahi 1591, Mughal province 1687, Nizam-ruled Hyderabad State 1724, annexed by India 1948 — and the seat of the Telangana Rebellion.
places.framing: Hyderabad's history runs through three regime layers. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded the city in 1591 as the Qutb Shahi capital; Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687, ending Qutb Shahi rule. The Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty, founded 1724 by a Mughal viceroy who broke away during the post-Aurangzeb succession crisis, ruled Hyderabad State as the largest princely state in British India until India's 1948 annexation (Operation Polo). The Telangana Rebellion (1946–51), led by the Communist Party against the Nizam's dora landlords, continued past the annexation against Nehru's army. Sarojini Naidu was a Hyderabad native; the city is also the home base of one of the major Indian Congress dynasties.

sources.label: Karen Leonard, Locating Home: India's Hyderabadis Abroad (2007)

places.name: Murshidabad
places.tooltip: Murshidabad — Bengal nawabi capital 1717–1772, EIC's first revenue base
places.summary: The Mughal-era Bengal nawabi seat that became the EIC's first revenue-generating capital after Plassey (1757) until Hastings shifted to Calcutta in 1772.
places.framing: Murshidabad was the capital of Bengal under the nawabs from 1717 (when Murshid Quli Khan moved the seat from Dhaka) until 1772 (when Warren Hastings centralised EIC government at Calcutta). The Battle of Plassey (1757) effectively ended nawabi independence; for the next fifteen years the EIC ran Bengal through Murshidabad's existing revenue apparatus while keeping the puppet nawab in place. Rammohan Roy worked here as a Persian-language munshi for the EIC in his late twenties — the experience that produced the Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (1803). The Sannyasi-Fakir rebels operated through this region; the Hastings administration that suppressed them was based here. The 1770 Bengal famine — in which an estimated ten million died and EIC tax collection actually rose — was the Murshidabad administration's defining failure.

sources.label: Rajat Kanta Ray, The Felt Community: Commonalty and Mentality before the Emergence of Indian Nationalism (2003)

places.name: Sabarmati Ashram
places.tooltip: Gandhi's ashram on the Sabarmati, Ahmedabad — 1917 to the Salt March (1930)
places.summary: Gandhi's institutional base 1917–33 — site of the Atmakatha (1925–29), launch of the Salt March (1930), abandoned after his vow not to return.
places.framing: Gandhi founded the ashram on the Sabarmati's west bank near Ahmedabad on 25 May 1915 (initial site), moving to the present location in 1917. From here he ran Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Atmakatha drafted week-by-week for Navjivan (1925–29), and the Salt March that began on 12 March 1930. After his arrest at Karadi the same year he vowed not to return to Sabarmati until independence; he kept the vow. The ashram was wound down as a satyagraha base in 1933 (handed to the Harijan Sevak Sangh) but remains the central architectural memorial of the post-1917 Gandhian programme. Tightly anchored: the place gathers events that happened on this single ashram footprint.

sources.label: Tridip Suhrud, An Autobiography or The Story of My Experiments with Truth: A Critical Edition (Penguin, 2018) — introduction on the ashram

places.name: Srirangapatna
places.tooltip: Srirangapatna — Hyder Ali / Tipu Sultan's island capital, 1761–1799
places.summary: The Cauvery-island fortress where Hyder Ali deposed the Wodeyars in 1761 and where Tipu Sultan was killed by EIC assault on 4 May 1799.
places.framing: Srirangapatna is a fortified island in the Cauvery, the capital of the Mysore Sultanate from Hyder Ali's 1761 coup against the Wodeyars until Tipu Sultan's death there on 4 May 1799 at the British storming of the fortress. The 1799 sack — which produced the cache of Tipu's papers including the Khwabnama, his sword, his throne, the famous mechanical tiger — was the founding plunder of the British India museum tradition. The Battle of Pollilur portraits (now in Edinburgh) and the Daria Daulat Bagh murals (Tipu's summer palace) are the most legible visual record of the Anglo-Mysore wars from the Mysore side. The Wodeyars were restored under British paramountcy from 1799 until the 1947 accession.

sources.label: Kate Brittlebank, Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy (1997)

places.name: Vellore
places.tooltip: Vellore Fort — site of 1806 sepoy mutiny; Tipu Sultan's family held here
places.summary: The Madras Presidency fort where Tipu Sultan's family was confined after 1799 and where the 1806 sepoy mutiny — 1857's structural rehearsal — broke out.
places.framing: Vellore Fort, built by the Vijayanagara empire in the 16th century, became a Madras Army cantonment and the place of confinement for Tipu Sultan's family after the 1799 sack of Srirangapatna. The 1806 sepoy mutiny — the Madras Native Infantry rising against new Christian-style headgear and grooming rules — broke out here on 10 July 1806 and was crushed within twelve hours by Colonel Gillespie's Arcot relief column, with approximately 350 sepoys executed (some by being blown from cannon). The mutiny's structural causes — coerced cultural assimilation, religious anxiety, princely-family-as-political-irritant — would recur in 1857 across north India. Vellore is the Madras Presidency's anchor in the corpus's pre-1857 rebellion arc.

sources.label: James W. Hoover, Men Without Hats (2007)

places.name: Daulatabad
places.tooltip: Daulatabad (Devagiri) — Tughlaq's failed second capital, Bahmani founding site
places.summary: Devagiri-renamed-Daulatabad: the hill-fort that anchored the Tughlaq capital-shift of 1327 and the Bahmani founding of 1347.
places.framing: Daulatabad began as Devagiri, the capital of the Yadava dynasty (12th c.–1317), conquered by Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur. Muhammad bin Tughlaq renamed it Daulatabad in 1327 and ordered the Delhi administrative class to relocate here — the most consequential failed urban planning act in subcontinental history, reversed within seven years. The same hill-fort then served as the brief 1347 coronation site for Hasan Gangu, founding the Bahmani Sultanate before the capital moved to Gulbarga. The fortress complex — multi-layered, with a moat carved into living rock and a single ascending pathway — is the most defensible large-scale fort in the Deccan and remained strategically relevant through the Mughal-Maratha contests of the 17th–18th centuries.

sources.label: Mahdi Husain, The Rise and Fall of Muhammad bin Tughluq (1938)

places.name: Gulbarga
places.tooltip: Gulbarga — Bahmani Sultanate capital 1347–1429
places.summary: Hasan Gangu shifted the Bahmani capital to Gulbarga shortly after the 1347 founding; the sultanate ruled the Deccan from here for eighty-two years.
places.framing: Gulbarga was the Bahmani capital from 1347 (shortly after Hasan Gangu's coronation at Daulatabad) until 1429, when Ahmad Shah Wali shifted the capital to Bidar. Across that century the Bahmanis built the Gulbarga Fort, the Jama Masjid (1367, modelled on the Cordoba mosque), and the dargah of the Sufi saint Khwaja Bande Nawaz, which remains the major pilgrimage site of the city. The Bahmani administrative innovations — the Persian-trained mulla-court, the jagir-based military assignment, the careful Hindu-Muslim political balance — were elaborated here. After the 1527 Bahmani fragmentation Gulbarga came under Bijapur (Adil Shahi) rule until Aurangzeb's 1686 annexation.

sources.label: H.K. Sherwani, The Bahmanis of the Deccan (1985)

places.name: Bidar
places.tooltip: Bidar — Bahmani Sultanate capital 1429–1527, then Barid Shahi
places.summary: Ahmad Shah Wali shifted the Bahmani capital to Bidar in 1429; the seat until 1527, then capital of the Barid Shahi successor sultanate until 1619.
places.framing: Ahmad Shah Wali Bahmani moved his capital from Gulbarga to Bidar in 1429, citing climate and water supply. Bidar's century as Bahmani capital (1429–1527) coincided with the kingdom's intellectual peak — the wazir Mahmud Gawan, a Persian merchant-administrator, ran the most centralised administration the Bahmanis ever achieved before factional intrigue (chiefly between the Deccani-born and Persian-born nobility) led to his execution in 1481. After the 1527 Bahmani fragmentation the city became capital of the Barid Shahi successor sultanate (1492–1619), one of the five Deccan Sultanates that Aurangzeb later annexed. The Bidar Fort, Mahmud Gawan's madrasa, and the Barid Shahi tombs constitute the surviving architectural record.

sources.label: H.K. Sherwani, The Bahmanis of the Deccan (1985)

places.name: Fatehpur Sikri
places.tooltip: Fatehpur Sikri — Akbar's planned capital 1571–1585
places.summary: Akbar's purpose-built capital west of Agra — abandoned within fourteen years for water-supply reasons; among the best-preserved Mughal urban sites.
places.framing: Akbar founded Fatehpur Sikri in 1571 to honour the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, whose blessing Akbar credited for the birth of his son Jahangir. The planned city — Diwan-i-Khas, Diwan-i-Am, the Buland Darwaza, the Jama Masjid, the Salim Chishti dargah, the Panch Mahal — was built in fourteen years on a sandstone ridge overlooking a lake. The Ibadat Khana religious debates that produced the Din-i-Ilahi were held here. By 1585 the lake was drying out and the water supply could not sustain the court; Akbar shifted the capital first to Lahore (for the northwest campaigns) and then back to Agra. Fatehpur Sikri was largely abandoned within the next two decades, leaving the city as a single-period architectural set-piece — among the most legible Mughal urban records anywhere.

sources.label: Ebba Koch, Mughal Architecture (1991), ch. 4

places.name: Madras
places.tooltip: Madras (Chennai) — EIC's first fortified Indian settlement, 1639
places.summary: Francis Day's 1639 acquisition from the Vijayanagara nayak became Fort St George — the EIC's first fortified Indian settlement and its southern capital.
places.framing: Francis Day, an EIC factor, acquired a strip of coast at Chennapatnam from the Vijayanagara-tributary Nayak of Chandragiri in August 1639. Fort St George, completed 1644, became the EIC's first fortified Indian settlement and the centre of EIC operations on the Coromandel coast. From 1684 Madras was a Presidency in its own right, equal to Bombay and Bengal. Robert Clive served his first commercial-then-military years here. Madras was the EIC's southern administrative capital until British India centralised at Calcutta after Hastings's 1772 reorganisation; it remained the Madras Presidency capital until 1947. Many of the colonial period's enduring institutions — the Madras Army, the University of Madras (1857), the Madras Presidency civil service — operated from here. The city was renamed Chennai in 1996.

sources.label: S. Muthiah, Madras Discovered (1981; rev. 2008 as Madras, Chennai: A 400-Year Record)

places.name: Bhopal
places.tooltip: Bhopal — Afghan-founded princely state 1723, Begum-ruled 1819–1926
places.summary: Founded 1723 by an Aurangzeb-army Afghan officer; uniquely ruled by four successive Begums for over a century from 1819.
places.framing: Bhopal was founded as an Afghan princely state in 1723 by Dost Muhammad Khan, an officer of Aurangzeb's army who consolidated a fragment of central India after the post-Aurangzeb collapse. From 1819 the state was ruled for over a century by four successive Begums (Qudsia, Sikandar, Shah Jahan, Sultan Jahan), making it unique among Indian princely states. The Begums modernised administration, promoted female education (Sultania Girls' School, 1903), and championed the All-India Muslim Ladies' Conference. Sultan Jahan abdicated in 1926; Bhopal acceded to India in 1949 after the abdication of her grandson Hamidullah Khan. The 1984 Union Carbide gas disaster gave Bhopal its modern global associations.

sources.label: Shaharyar M. Khan, The Begums of Bhopal (2000)

places.name: Anandpur Sahib
places.tooltip: Anandpur Sahib — Khalsa founded here on Baisakhi, 30 March 1699
places.summary: Punjab town founded 1665 by Guru Tegh Bahadur; the site of the Khalsa's founding by Guru Gobind Singh on Baisakhi 1699.
places.framing: Anandpur Sahib was founded by the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur, in 1665 on land purchased from the Raja of Bilaspur, originally as Chakk Nanaki. The town became the seat of the Sikh Gurus' political-military leadership; Guru Gobind Singh established the Khalsa here on Baisakhi (30 March) 1699 — the founding act of organised Sikh political life. The Five Beloved (Panj Pyare) initiation ritual and the Khalsa code (rehat) were promulgated at Anandpur. Mughal-Hill Raja sieges of Anandpur (1701–1705) eventually forced the Guru to abandon the town; the surviving Khalsa regrouped at Damdama Sahib. The Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib gurdwara at Anandpur, marking the founding spot, is one of the five Sikh takhts.

sources.label: J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1990)

places.name: Raigad
places.tooltip: Raigad Fort — Shivaji's coronation 1674, first Maratha capital
places.summary: Western Ghats hill-fort that Shivaji renamed from Rairi and chose as his coronation site (6 June 1674) — the founding capital of the Maratha state.
places.framing: Raigad — originally Rairi, captured by Shivaji from Chandrarao More of Javli in 1656 — was renamed and developed as the Maratha capital from 1664. Shivaji's formal coronation as Chhatrapati was held at Raigad on 6 June 1674, a deliberate Hindu sovereign-claim act with full Vedic ritual and the construction of the Singhasan Devi temple. Shivaji ruled from Raigad until his death there on 3 April 1680. Sambhaji and Rajaram subsequently held the fort until 1689 when Aurangzeb's forces under Zulfiqar Khan captured it; the Mughal occupation lasted until the early 18th century when the Marathas retook it. The Peshwa-era capital shift to Pune in 1714 ended Raigad's political role; the fort remained a Maratha symbol through the colonial period.

sources.label: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (1993)

places.name: Thiruvananthapuram
places.tooltip: Thiruvananthapuram — Travancore capital 1745–1947, then Kerala state capital
places.summary: Travancore capital from 1745 under Marthanda Varma; the city of the Padmanabhaswamy temple to which the kingdom was formally dedicated in 1750.
places.framing: Thiruvananthapuram became the Travancore capital in 1745 when Marthanda Varma shifted the seat from Padmanabhapuram. The 1750 trippadidanam ceremony — the king's formal dedication of the kingdom to Sri Padmanabhaswamy — made the rulers nominal regents (dasa) of the deity, a sovereignty-claim that survived British paramountcy intact. The Padmanabhaswamy temple's 2011 vault discovery (estimated US$22 billion in gold and gems) is the largest known temple treasure ever found. Travancore acceded to India on 27 August 1947 after C.P. Ramaswami Iyer's brief independence bid; the city was the capital of Travancore-Cochin (1949–56) and then of Kerala state from 1956. Renamed officially from Trivandrum to Thiruvananthapuram in 1991.

sources.label: Robin Jeffrey, The Decline of Nayar Dominance (1976)

places.name: Hampi
places.tooltip: Hampi — Vijayanagara capital 1336–1565, sacked after Talikota
places.summary: Vijayanagara capital on the south bank of the Tungabhadra — at its peak under Krishna Deva Raya among the largest cities in the world; sacked after Talikota.
places.framing: Hampi was founded as the Vijayanagara capital on 18 April 1336 by Harihara and Bukka Sangama in the Tungabhadra valley, on a granite-strewn landscape that had earlier been a Pampa-Hampi shrine site associated with the Ramayana's Kishkindha. Across two and a quarter centuries the city grew to perhaps 500,000 inhabitants — the second-largest in the world by some 16th-century estimates, after Beijing. Persian and European travellers (Abdur Razzak 1443, Domingo Paes 1520, Fernão Nunes 1530s) recorded the markets, the four-storey royal palaces, the Vitthala temple's musical pillars, the Pampapathi shrine, the Mahanavami platform on which Krishna Deva Raya held the dasara reviews. The Deccan Sultanate alliance sacked Hampi over five months after Talikota (1565); the city was never reoccupied. The ruins — covering 41 square kilometres — are India's largest archaeological site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986).

sources.label: John M. Fritz & George Michell, Hampi Vijayanagara (Marg, 2008)

places.name: Bijapur
places.tooltip: Bijapur — Adil Shahi capital 1490–1686, then under Mughal rule
places.summary: Adil Shahi sultanate capital from 1490 to Aurangzeb's 1686 annexation — among the most architecturally rich Bahmani-successor cities.
places.framing: Bijapur (today Vijayapura, Karnataka) was the Adil Shahi capital from 1490 to 1686 — 196 years, the longest-lived of the five Bahmani-successor sultanates. The city's architecture is the most legible Adil Shahi record: the Gol Gumbaz of Mohammed Adil Shah (completed 1656) is the second-largest dome in the world (44m diameter) and contains the famous whispering gallery; the Ibrahim Rauza (1626) is among the most ornate Indo-Islamic mausoleums; the Jama Masjid (started 1576), the citadel, and the cluster of saint dargahs constitute a major Indian Islamic heritage site. Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur in October 1686 after a fifteen-month siege; the city declined under Mughal then EIC rule. Population peaked at around 800,000 in the 17th century; today it is a regional district headquarters.

sources.label: Helen Philon (ed.), Silent Splendour: Palaces of the Deccan, 14th–19th Centuries (2010)

places.name: Golconda
places.tooltip: Golconda — Qutb Shahi capital 1518–1591, diamond-rich; fell to Aurangzeb 1687
places.summary: Qutb Shahi capital from 1518 until 1591 (when Hyderabad was founded); the diamond-trade fortress that fell to Aurangzeb after an eight-month siege in 1687.
places.framing: Golconda was the Qutb Shahi capital from 1518, when Sultan-Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk founded the dynasty, until 1591, when Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded the new city of Hyderabad twelve kilometres east. The fortress remained the seat of state administration and the treasury — its diamond mines at Kollur (the source of the Koh-i-Noor, Hope Diamond, and Daria-i-Noor) made Golconda synonymous with wealth in 17th-century Persian and European travel literature. The Qutb Shahi tombs north of the fort form a coherent dynastic necropolis. Aurangzeb's siege of Golconda (January–October 1687) was the final phase of his Deccan campaign — the fort fell on 21 September 1687 after Mughal forces bribed the gate guards. The Qutb Shahi treasury became part of Aurangzeb's; the dynasty ended; Hyderabad eventually became the Asaf Jahi (Nizam) capital in the 18th century.

sources.label: George Michell & Mark Zebrowski, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates (Cambridge New History of India I.7, 1999)

places.name: Mysore
places.tooltip: Mysore — Wodeyar capital 1399–1610 and 1799–1947
places.summary: Wodeyar capital from 1399 (with Srirangapatna interlude) — modern princely city of southern Karnataka.
places.framing: Mysore (Mysuru) was the original Wodeyar capital from 1399 until Raja Wodeyar I shifted to Srirangapatna in 1610 for strategic-defensive reasons. After the EIC's 1799 restoration of Krishnaraja III Wodeyar following Tipu Sultan's defeat, Mysore became the capital of the restored princely state and remained so until 1947. The Amba Vilas (Mysore Palace), rebuilt in 1912 after a 1897 fire, is among the most photographed Indian palaces. Mysore became famous in the 19th–20th centuries for the Dasara festival, the Mysore school of painting, sandalwood and silk craft industries, and the reformist administration of the Wodeyar maharajas (universal primary education from 1843, Mysore University founded 1916). The city merged into Karnataka state in 1956.

sources.label: James Manor, Political Change in an Indian State: Mysore 1917–1955 (1977)

places.name: Charaideo
places.tooltip: Charaideo — Sukapha's first Ahom capital, 1228
places.summary: Upper-Assam capital founded by Sukapha in 1228 — the first Ahom seat; today the site of the Maidam royal burial mounds.
places.framing: Sukapha founded Charaideo as the first Ahom capital in 1228 after his crossing of the Patkai from Mong Mao. Across six centuries (1228–1826) the Ahom capital shifted across upper Assam — to Charagua, Garhgaon (1540), Rangpur, Jorhat — but Charaideo retained ritual primacy as the sacred founding-site and as the location of the Maidam royal burial mounds where Ahom swargadeos and senior nobles were interred. The 90+ surviving Maidams of Charaideo were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024 — the first cultural heritage site from Northeast India on the list. The site is in modern Sivasagar district of Assam, about 28 km east of Sivasagar town.

sources.label: Edward Gait, A History of Assam (1906; rev. 1933)

places.name: Imphal
places.tooltip: Imphal — Manipur capital across regimes; site of 1891 hangings, 1944 WWII battle
places.summary: Manipur capital across Meitei kingdom, princely state, and modern republic — site of 1891 Bir Tikendrajit's hanging and the 1944 Battle of Imphal.
places.framing: Imphal was the Manipur capital under the Meitei (Ningthouja) line of kings from at least the 7th century, surviving the Burmese 1819–1826 Devastation, the 1891 Anglo-Manipur War (after which Bir Tikendrajit and Thangal General were publicly hanged in the city's Polo Ground), and the WWII Battle of Imphal (March–July 1944) — the latter the high water of Japanese-INA penetration into India and a key turning point in the Burma campaign. Manipur acceded to India 21 September 1949; Imphal became state capital with statehood in 1972. Modern Imphal anchors the Northeast's longest-running ethnic-political contest between Meitei (valley), Naga (northern hills), and Kuki-Zo (southern hills) populations.

sources.label: Lal Dena, History of Modern Manipur 1826–1949 (1991)

places.name: Yuksom
places.tooltip: Yuksom — Sikkim's first Chogyal consecrated 1642 at the Norbugang throne
places.summary: Western Sikkim site of the 1642 consecration of Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal — Sikkim's sacred founding-site.
places.framing: Yuksom in west Sikkim was the consecration site where three Tibetan Nyingma lamas — Lhatsun Chenpo, Kathok Kuntu Zangpo, and Ngadak Sempa Chenpo — anointed Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim in 1642. The Norbugang Coronation Throne, a four-trunked pine under which the ceremony was held, remains the sacred founding-site of the Sikkimese state. Yuksom served as the first Sikkimese capital briefly before the Chogyals shifted to Rabdentse, then Tumlong, then Gangtok (from 1894). The Dubdi Monastery, founded by Lhatsun Chenpo c. 1701, and the surrounding Khangchendzonga National Park constitute a Buddhist cultural landscape that supports modern Sikkimese identity-politics.

sources.label: Saul Mullard, Opening the Hidden Land: State Formation and the Construction of Sikkimese History (2011)

places.name: Gangtok
places.tooltip: Gangtok — Sikkim Chogyal capital from 1894, then Indian state capital from 1975
places.summary: Sikkim's capital from 1894 (Chogyal Thutob Namgyal's shift from Tumlong) to the present — 1975 merger into India and modern state capital.
places.framing: Gangtok became the Sikkim capital in 1894 when Chogyal Thutob Namgyal shifted the seat from Tumlong, partly under British pressure to accommodate the new political-officer presence at Sikkim's interface with British India and Tibet. Across the next eighty years the city was the seat of the Namgyal dynasty's last four Chogyals, the British political-agent residency (1889 onwards), the post-1947 Indian protectorate (1950 Treaty of Peace), and finally the merger that made Sikkim India's 22nd state in 1975. Gangtok has remained state capital since. The Royal Palace, Enchey Monastery (1909), and the Tsuk-La-Khang (royal chapel) constitute the principal architectural legacy of the Chogyal period.

sources.label: Sunanda K. Datta-Ray, Smash and Grab: Annexation of Sikkim (1984)

places.name: Agartala
places.tooltip: Agartala — Tripura Manikya capital 1850s onwards, then state capital
places.summary: Tripura's capital under the late Manikya dynasty (from 1850s); merged into India 1949; modern Tripura state capital from 1972.
places.framing: Agartala became the principal Manikya capital in the mid-19th century, succeeding Old Agartala (Khayerpur, the earlier Manikya seat near the Burma-now-Bangladesh frontier). Maharaja Bir Chandra Manikya (r. 1862–1896) extensively rebuilt Agartala — the Ujjayanta Palace (1901, completed under his successor), the Jagannath temple, the modern street grid. Tripura acceded to India on 15 October 1949 under the regency of Kanchan Prabha Devi (the Manikya queen-regent for the minor heir). Agartala became a Union Territory capital, then full state capital with Tripura statehood in 1972. The city sits less than 2 kilometres from the Bangladesh border and was the largest Indian relief base for refugees during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War.

sources.label: Jagadis Gan-Chaudhuri, A Constitutional History of Tripura (1980)

places.name: Pataliputra
places.tooltip: Pataliputra (Patna) — Mauryan, Sunga, Gupta, Pala capital
places.summary: Magadha capital from the 5th c. BCE; capital of the Mauryan, Sunga, and Gupta empires; later Pala seat — north India's longest-running ancient capital.
places.framing: Pataliputra was founded by Ajatasattu of Magadha as a fort at the Ganga-Sone confluence in the 5th century BCE; expanded into the imperial capital under his successors. Across nearly a millennium it served as capital to the Nanda dynasty, the Mauryan Empire (322–185 BCE), the Sunga dynasty (185–73 BCE), the Gupta Empire (320–550 CE), and (with Vikramashila) the Pala Empire (8th–12th c.). Megasthenes recorded the city in the 3rd century BCE as fifteen kilometres long with sixty-four gates and 570 towers — likely the largest city in the world at the time. Faxian visited in c. 405 CE and recorded the still-functioning Mauryan-era hospital and palaces. Bakhtiyar Khilji's 1193 sack ended Pataliputra's institutional continuity; the Ganga's eastward shift across centuries silted over much of the ancient site. Modern Patna stands on the same footprint; archaeological excavations at Kumrahar have recovered the Mauryan pillared hall.

sources.label: Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002)

places.name: Sarnath
places.tooltip: Sarnath — Buddha's first sermon; Ashokan Lion Capital + pillar
places.summary: Site of the Buddha's first sermon (Dharmachakra Pravartana, c. 528 BCE) and Ashoka's Lion Capital — the modern Indian state emblem.
places.framing: Sarnath, in the deer park (mrigadava) outside Varanasi, is where Siddhartha Gautama delivered his first sermon (Dharmachakra Pravartana — 'turning the wheel of dhamma') to his five former ascetic companions, c. 528 BCE according to traditional dating. The site became one of the four principal Buddhist pilgrimage centres alongside Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, and Kushinagar. Ashoka erected a pillar at Sarnath bearing his Schism Edict and topped by the four-lion capital — recovered intact by colonial archaeologists in 1904 and adopted as the State Emblem of India in 1950. The wheel from the lion capital appears on the Indian national flag. The Mulagandhakuti Vihara (originally Mauryan, expanded by Kushans, restored under Mahabodhi Society in 1931) and the Dhamekh Stupa (5th c. CE Gupta-era reconstruction of an earlier Mauryan stupa) anchor the surviving architectural site.

sources.label: Vidya Dehejia, Indian Art (1997), ch. on Mauryan and Buddhist sculpture

places.name: Bodh Gaya
places.tooltip: Bodh Gaya — site of the Buddha's enlightenment under the Bodhi tree
places.summary: Site where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, c. 534 BCE — Buddhism's most sacred location.
places.framing: Bodh Gaya is the site where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa) after 49 days of meditation, c. 534 BCE in traditional reckoning. The Mahabodhi Temple complex — its core 5th–6th century Gupta-era brick structure built over an earlier Ashokan shrine — surrounds the present Bodhi tree, traditionally a direct descendant of the original. Ashoka visited Bodh Gaya in c. 260 BCE and erected the diamond throne (Vajrasana) marker; his daughter Sanghamitta is said to have taken a sapling of the original Bodhi tree to Sri Lanka, where its descendant still grows at Anuradhapura. The site declined after Bakhtiyar Khilji's sack of nearby Nalanda 1193 and the spread of Islam in eastern India; the temple was rediscovered by Burmese pilgrims in the 19th century and restored by Alexander Cunningham. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2002); Buddhism's most sacred location.

sources.label: Geri H. Malandra, Unfolding a Mandala: The Buddhist Cave Temples at Ellora (1993) — context

places.name: Sanchi
places.tooltip: Sanchi — Ashokan stupa cluster, Sunga-era toranas
places.summary: Hilltop Buddhist stupa complex founded by Ashoka c. 250 BCE; the Great Stupa's Satavahana-era toranas are India's most celebrated early Buddhist sculpture.
places.framing: Sanchi was founded by Ashoka around 250 BCE as a Buddhist monastic centre — the Great Stupa (Stupa No. 1) is the earliest surviving large stupa in India. Under Sunga and Satavahana patronage in the 1st century BCE the Great Stupa was enlarged with its present stone facing and surrounded by a balustrade; the four ornately carved toranas (gateways) added in the 1st century BCE depict Jataka tales and Buddhist symbology in some of the most accomplished early Indian narrative-relief sculpture. The site flourished as a monastic centre through the Gupta period (the Vihara No. 51 is 5th-c.) and into the 12th c., then declined. Cunningham's 1851 archaeological recovery (he discovered Sariputta and Mahamoggallana's relics in Stupa No. 3) launched modern Indian Buddhist archaeology. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1989). Ashoka's regional capital was at nearby Vidisha; his queen Devi (mother of Mahinda) was a Vidisha merchant's daughter.

sources.label: John Marshall, A Guide to Sanchi (1918; rev. 1955)
Vidya Dehejia, Discourse in Early Buddhist Art: Visual Narratives of India (1997)

places.name: Ujjain
places.tooltip: Ujjain — Avanti capital, Vikramaditya's seat, Indian prime meridian
places.summary: Avanti mahajanapada capital from the 6th c. BCE; Gupta winter capital under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya; Vedic prime-meridian timekeeping centre.
places.framing: Ujjain (ancient Avantika) was the capital of the Avanti mahajanapada from the 6th century BCE — among the major north Indian states the Buddha's life encountered. Through successive periods it served as: a Mauryan provincial capital (Ashoka was governor here as crown prince before his accession); the Western Kshatrapa Saka capital (1st–4th c. CE); the Gupta winter capital under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (4th–5th c.) and traditional seat of his navaratna court of Sanskrit literati; and a Paramara capital in the early-medieval period. Ujjain is the traditional Indian prime meridian — Hindu astronomical timekeeping (the Surya Siddhanta) takes Ujjain's longitude as zero, since the Tropic of Cancer crosses very near the city. The 12-yearly Simhastha Kumbh Mela on the Shipra river is among the four major Kumbh sites; the Mahakaleshwar temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva. Modern Ujjain is in Madhya Pradesh.

sources.label: Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India (2002)

places.name: Nalanda
places.tooltip: Nalanda Mahavihara — Buddhist university 5th–12th c.; Bakhtiyar Khilji 1193
places.summary: Buddhist university in Magadha founded c. 5th c. CE under Gupta patronage; Xuanzang's residency 635–640; destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji c. 1193.
places.framing: Nalanda Mahavihara was the largest Buddhist monastic university of the early-medieval Indian world — founded under Gupta patronage in the 5th century CE, expanded continuously under successive Pala emperors (Dharmapala, Devapala) from the 8th–11th centuries, and destroyed in Bakhtiyar Khilji's c. 1193 raid. Xuanzang's mid-7th-century account records 10,000 monks, 1,500 teachers, 108 monasteries, and three libraries (Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, Ratnaranjaka) holding millions of palm-leaf manuscripts. Faxian had visited the predecessor site two centuries earlier; the Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvamin's 1235 account confirms the institution survived in reduced form through the 13th century. The site lay buried until Cunningham's 1861 excavations; the brick stupa-vihara complex visible today is among India's most extensive archaeological remains. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016). The modern Nalanda University (founded 2014) is a partial revival initiative.

sources.label: Hartmut Scharfe, Education in Ancient India (2002), ch. on monastic universities

places.name: Kanauj
places.tooltip: Kanauj — Harsha's capital 606–647; prize of the Tripartite Struggle
places.summary: Harsha of Kanauj's capital from 606 to 647; the symbolic-imperial centre that the Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas contested for 150 years.
places.framing: Kanauj (Sanskrit Kanyakubja) was Harsha's imperial capital from c. 611 to 647 CE — the political successor to Pataliputra in the post-Gupta period. After Harsha's death without heir, Kanauj became the symbolic prize of the Tripartite Struggle (c. 783–950 CE) between the Pratiharas (north), Palas (east), and Rashtrakutas (Deccan). The Pratiharas eventually consolidated control under Bhoja I (r. 836–885) and held it until Mahmud of Ghazni's 1018 sack accelerated the dynasty's collapse. The Gahadavalas of Kanauj (c. 1090–1194) were the last major Hindu dynasty there before the Ghurid conquest. Modern Kanauj is a town in Uttar Pradesh known for its perfume (ittar) industry — a survival of the Mughal-era distillation trade.

sources.label: Brajadulal Chattopadhyaya, The Making of Early Medieval India (1994; rev. 2012)

places.name: Tanjore
places.tooltip: Tanjore (Thanjavur) — Imperial Chola capital, 985–1279; Brihadishvara temple
places.summary: Imperial Chola capital under Rajaraja and Rajendra; site of the 1010 Brihadishvara temple — among the longest South Indian capital cities.
places.framing: Tanjore was the Imperial Chola capital from Vijayalaya's 9th-century consolidation through Rajaraja I (985–1014) and Rajendra I (1014–1044) — the high water of South Indian imperial-period building. The Brihadishvara temple (1010) is the architectural monument; the surrounding city housed the Chola court, the Saraswati Mahal Library (later Maratha foundation but on Chola foundations), and the goldsmith and bronze-casting workshops that produced the Chola bronze tradition. Rajendra I shifted the capital to Gangaikonda Cholapuram c. 1025 after the northern campaigns; later Chola rulers (Kulottunga I onwards) returned the seat to Tanjore. After the Chola decline (c. 1279) the city served as a Pandya, Vijayanagara-Nayaka, and finally Maratha (Bhonsle) capital from 1674 — Sarfoji II Bhonsle (r. 1798–1832) collected the great Saraswati Mahal manuscript library before British annexation in 1855. Modern Thanjavur preserves the Chola monumental and bronze-tradition centre.

sources.label: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Cōḷas (1935; rev. 1955)

places.name: Somnath
places.tooltip: Somnath — Saurashtra Shiva temple; sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni 1026
places.summary: Coastal Saurashtra Shiva temple; one of the twelve Jyotirlingas; sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni 1026; rebuilt repeatedly, most recently 1947–1951.
places.framing: Somnath, on the Saurashtra coast facing the Arabian Sea, is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva — the most sacred set of Shaivite pilgrimage sites in the Hindu tradition. The wealthiest Hindu temple of the early-medieval period (under Solanki patronage), it became Mahmud of Ghazni's most consequential target — his January 1026 raid sacked the temple and carried off treasure traditionally valued at 20 million dinars. The destruction-rebuilding-destruction cycle ran across the next eight centuries: rebuilt under Bhima I Solanki (mid-11th c.), sacked by Alauddin Khalji's general (1299), rebuilt under Mahipala I, sacked by Muzaffar Shah of Gujarat (1395) and again by Aurangzeb (1665). The current temple is the 1947–1951 reconstruction promoted by Sardar Patel (against Nehru's expressed reservations) and inaugurated by President Rajendra Prasad in 1951 — a politically charged act in the early years of the Republic. Romila Thapar's Somanatha (2004) is the standard modern critical history of the temple's contested narrative.

sources.label: Romila Thapar, Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004)

places.name: Ayodhya
places.tooltip: Ayodhya — Ramayana setting; Babri Masjid demolition 1992; 2019 SC verdict
places.summary: Sarayu-river city of the Ramayana tradition; site of the 1528 Babri Masjid, its 1992 demolition, and the 2019 Supreme Court site-award verdict.
places.framing: Ayodhya on the Sarayu river in eastern Uttar Pradesh is the traditional setting of the Ramayana — birthplace of the deity Ram in Hindu tradition. Archaeological work at the city dates significant occupation from the 7th century BCE; the city served as a Maurya-era then Gupta-era Buddhist-Jain-Hindu pilgrimage centre. The Babri Masjid, built 1528 (attributed to Mir Baqi under Babur), stood on a site Hindu tradition identified as Ram Janmabhoomi (Ram's birthplace) — disputed continuously through colonial-era court cases and the post-Independence Ram Janmabhoomi movement. The mosque's demolition on 6 December 1992 by an estimated 150,000 kar sevaks, the subsequent communal riots (~2,000 dead) and the 1993 Bombay blasts, the Liberhan Commission inquiry, and the 2019 Supreme Court verdict awarding the disputed 2.77-acre site to the Ram Janmabhoomi trust — while finding no archaeological evidence of a demolished temple directly underlying the mosque — constitute the contested modern political-religious history.

sources.label: Hans Bakker, Ayodhya (1986)

places.name: Puri
places.tooltip: Puri — Jagannath temple seat, c. 12th c. onward; chronicled in the Madala Panji
places.summary: The Eastern Ganga and Suryavamsi capital that became — and remained — the institutional and ritual centre of the Jagannath cult on India's east coast.
places.framing: Puri's institutional anchor is the Jagannath Temple, founded under the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga in the early 12th century and continuously functional since. The temple's institutional record — the Madala Panji palm-leaf chronicles maintained by the Karana scribal family — covers four centuries of royal patronage, festival administration, and ritual reform across Suryavamsi, Mughal-era, Maratha, and British rule. The Rath Yatra is among the largest annual ritual processions in subcontinental religious life. Puri sits within the Khurda kingdom whose 1817 Paika Rebellion was the major early Odia anti-EIC rising. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spent his last years here (died 1534); Adi Shankara established the Govardhana matha here in the 8th century — making Puri one of the four cardinal Hindu monastic seats.

sources.label: Hermann Kulke, Kings and Cults (1993), ch. on Jagannath
